Lidole (Oreochromis lidole) is a large-bodied cichlid endemic to Lake Malawi, and recent field surveys have provided a comprehensive set of life-history benchmarks for this species. Young hatch from eggs with a diameter of approximately 2.5 mm, and the resulting yolk-sac larvae have a wet weight at birth of just 0.0082 grams [Wwb = 0.0082 grams], a value that reflects the modest provisioning of the egg. As these lecithotrophic larvae absorb their yolk reserves and transition to exogenous feeding, they begin a phase of rapid somatic growth. Under the stable thermal conditions of the lake, which average 28 °C [T = 28 °C], the maximum recorded longevity for this species is approximately nine years [am = approximately nine years], a lifespan that is relatively extended for a tilapiine cichlid and likely reflects the low natural mortality rates characteristic of a large lacustrine predator. The ultimate total length attained by adults reaches 38 centimeters [Li = 38 centimeters], a size that places O. lidole among the largest members of its genus in the lake basin.

As individuals progress through the juvenile and sub-adult stages, growth trajectories are strongly influenced by the thermal regime of the species' preferred rocky habitat at 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. Under these conditions, puberty is attained when fish reach a total length at puberty of 29.9 centimeters [Lp = 29.9 centimeters], a milestone that corresponds to the onset of gonadal recrudescence and the activation of the HPG axis. The corresponding wet weight at puberty for individuals at this length is 233.1 grams [Wwp = 233.1 grams], a body mass that indicates substantial energy reserves have been accumulated prior to the initiation of reproductive activity. This size at maturity is considerably larger than that reported for congeneric species such as Oreochromis mossambicus, which typically become reproductively viable at a far smaller body size, suggesting that O. lidole delays maturation to support a more competitive adult niche. The duration of this pre-reproductive growth phase reflects a life-history strategy oriented toward achieving a competitive size advantage before first spawning.

The maximum adult body mass recorded for O. lidole in Lake Malawi is 678.9 grams [Wwi = 678.9 grams], an ultimate wet weight that corresponds to the asymptotic size derived from growth curve analyses of large, sexually mature individuals. This value is notably greater than the 233.1 grams [Wwp = 233.1 grams] typical at puberty, indicating that substantial somatic growth continues well after the onset of reproductive maturity. Females in particular invest considerable energy in both continued growth and annual reproductive bouts, a pattern that is consistent with an iteroparous, income-breeding strategy common among lacustrine cichlids. Field collections of gravid females have revealed that a single spawning event typically yields around 730 eggs [N_R_i = single spawning event typically yields around 730 eggs], a clutch size that places O. lidole among the more fecund tilapiines in the lake. At a sustained water temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], females are capable of producing about one such clutch per year [F_R_i = about one such clutch per year], so the annual reproductive output is substantial, ensuring high recruitment potential in favorable years.

Ecological comparisons with Oreochromis andersonii, a related species from the Zambezi system, provide useful context for interpreting the reproductive physiology of O. lidole. Both species achieve maximum clutch sizes of roughly 730 eggs, but the daily reproductive rate in O. lidole is constrained by the annual frequency of spawning events rather than by clutch volume alone. The sustained water temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C] in Lake Malawi's shallow littoral zones supports a relatively high metabolic rate and a short inter-spawning interval, allowing females to complete gonadal recrudescence and vitellogenesis within a single annual cycle. The total length at puberty of 29.9 centimeters [Lp = 29.9 centimeters] is a critical threshold; below this size, individuals remain in a pre-reproductive juvenile state and do not initiate gametogenesis. This size-based maturation schedule buffers the population against recruitment failure during years of low food availability, as only individuals that have achieved sufficient somatic reserves are permitted to invest in egg production.

Long-term mark-recapture studies have confirmed that the maximum lifespan of O. lidole in Lake Malawi is approximately nine years [am = approximately nine years], with individuals maintained at the average lake temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C] showing no evidence of reproductive senescence until their final year. The ultimate total length of 38 centimeters [Li = 38 centimeters] is typically reached between the sixth and seventh year of life, after which growth slows considerably as energy is diverted increasingly toward gonadal development. The wet weight at birth of 0.0082 grams [Wwb = 0.0082 grams] is remarkably small relative to the adult mass, indicating a nearly 83,000-fold increase in body mass over the lifespan. The ultimate wet weight of 678.9 grams [Wwi = 678.9 grams] represents a plateau in somatic investment, beyond which individuals channel most available energy into annual reproductive effort. These life-history traits collectively characterize O. lidole as a K-selected strategist within the cichlid assemblage of Lake Malawi, prioritizing longevity and competitive adult size over rapid generational turnover.
